analysis.title: Living on the Edge: The Rise of Distributed Power
key_insights: Morgan Stanley argues the AI buildout is colliding with a grid that cannot deliver power fast enough. Combined with the shift from training to inference and political pushback against mega-campus data centers, it expects a structural shift toward distributed behind-the-meter (BTM) power.

Time-to-power is becoming as important as cost-of-power. MS introduces the Stranded Compute Adjusted Cost of Power (SCACP), which adds the monetized cost of idle GPUs to the levelized cost of electricity (LCOE).

In MS's composite BTM ranking today, Bloom Energy's solid-oxide fuel cell (SOFC) ranks #1 (4.5/5), BorgWarner's micro turbine generator #2 (3.7), FTAI's aeroderivative turbine #3 (3.4), fast-start reciprocating gas engines #4 (3.3) and industrial gas turbines #5 (1.8).

The ranking depends on time-to-power. With no time premium (2030 view), reciprocating gas engines rank #1 and SOFC #2 (both 3.8), and the range of scores narrows. The market debate is how long the acute time-to-power problem lasts.
MS forecasts a ~120 GW, or $240bn, BTM power equipment TAM through 2029 (77 GW data center plus 40 GW commercial & industrial).

US data center power shortfall: 160 GW of incremental demand for 2026-2029, with 22 GW under construction with grid connection, 36 GW of available grid capacity, 23 GW of BTM equipment already procured, leaving a 77 GW shortfall.

BTM power is not just a bridge solution. Data center demand drives manufacturing scale and lower costs for fuel cells, turbines, microgrids and storage, which opens commercial & industrial (C&I) demand. MS estimates 40 GW of incremental C&I demand through 2029 and ~10 GW a year through 2030.
The grid still matters. MS thinks CCGTs or the grid are best suited to 1 GW+ training mega-sites, while smaller inference nodes favor modular solutions such as fuel cells and small turbines.

Storage is the balancing layer. MS expects US energy storage (ESS) demand to grow from 57 GWh in 2025 to ~280 GWh in 2030, ~60% for data centers, with hybrid setups (fast thermal source plus storage) becoming the default onsite design.
Virtual power plants (VPPs) are scaling. On September 9, Sunrun and Tesla coordinated more than 140,000 home batteries to deliver over 580 MW to the California grid for a three-hour dispatch.

Sunrun, Tesla and Renew Home signed a non-binding framework in June 2026 to aggregate more than 16 GW of flexible capacity for utilities and hyperscalers, with 300+ MW of flexible resources in Virginia.

Supply/demand debate: MS estimates 149 GW of primary gas power equipment supply by 2030 versus ~150 GW of data center demand. Its table shows a supply surplus of 19.9 GW in 2027 and 4.8 GW in 2028, flipping to shortages of 15.1 GW in 2029 and 29.2 GW in 2030.

Pricing and terms support suppliers. Prices are still rising for large-frame and industrial gas turbines, slot-reservation down payments are up to 25% for 2030 delivery, and INIO and CAT are fully booked through 2028.

Political pushback is a tailwind for BTM. About $156 billion of data center projects were cancelled or delayed in 2025 and $130 billion in 1Q26. Texas is auditing 474 GW of pending ERCOT requests, and Pennsylvania ended fast-track permitting. MS says most efforts aim to slow, not reverse, the buildout.
Physical AI (vehicles, robots) creates a distributed compute and power layer. MS estimates robot/EV compute capacity could reach ~1.0 TW by 2040.

trade_ideas.description: Long Overweight-rated onsite power equipment suppliers: Bloom Energy (BE), BorgWarner (BWA), FTAI Aviation (FTAI), INNIO (INIO), ERock (EROC), Cummins (CMI), Baker Hughes (BKR), Rolls Royce (RR)
trade_ideas.rationale: BTM power is a structural shift as the grid cannot deliver power fast enough, and supply is expected to fall short of demand by 2029-2030.
trade_ideas.risk: Oversupply from new entrants, or time-to-power constraints easing so that cost matters more than speed.

trade_ideas.description: Long onsite power developers: Solaris (SEI), Liberty (LBRT), Halliburton (HAL), Williams (WMB)
trade_ideas.rationale: 23 GW of BTM equipment is already procured by these developers for deployment at data center sites.

trade_ideas.description: Long ESS/VPP providers: Tesla (TSLA), Ford (F), Fluence (FLNC), BorgWarner (BWA), Sunrun (RUN)
trade_ideas.rationale: Storage is the balancing layer for onsite power, and VPPs showed power-plant-scale dispatch in California.

risk_factors: Time-to-power constraints could ease, which would narrow the advantage of fast-deploying technologies. With no time premium, reciprocating engines overtake SOFC.
Supply may be oversupplied if new entrants and non-data-center equipment add capacity, though MS thinks 2030 supply is potentially overstated and demand understated.
Political backlash and data center moratoriums, though MS says these mostly slow rather than reverse the buildout.
SMRs have no commercially available product today and face 5-10 year permitting and construction timelines.
Solar plus storage is limited behind the meter by land needs and intermittency.

The composite ranking depends on MS's weightings (50% SCACP, 15% noise/NIMBY, 15% technology maturity, 10% each for load following and emissions). Developers with different priorities could rank technologies differently.
Morgan Stanley discloses investment banking and other relationships with many of the covered companies.
charts_described: Exhibit 2/10 shows the US data center power shortfall through 2029 (midpoint scenario): 160.0 GW demand, 21.8 GW under construction, 36.2 GW grid access, 22.8 GW BTM turbines/engines in backlog, 2.8 GW nuclear plant siting, leaving a 76.5 GW net shortfall.
Exhibit 7/20 shows US energy storage demand rising to 280 GWh by 2030, with non-data-center demand of 57 GWh in 2025 and about 110 GWh in 2030, and data center ESS demand reaching 169 GWh.
Exhibit 9/25 shows incremental US C&I demand rising from 9.8 GW in 2027E to 13.3 GW in 2035E.
Exhibit 12/3 shows SCACP in $/MWh as BTM LCOE plus a stranded compute premium, with grid power at the highest SCACP of $323.
geopolitical: Local and state political pushback against data centers (Texas ERCOT audit of 474 GW of requests, Virginia Rider T1 order, Pennsylvania executive order ending fast-track permitting) ahead of the midterm elections.
Reshoring of US manufacturing is described as a bipartisan effort that adds electricity demand.

tension_points.bull_case: MS estimates 149 GW of gas power equipment supply against ~150 GW of data center demand by 2030, with a 29.2 GW shortage in 2030 once 20% redundancy is included. Prices are rising, down payments are up to 25% and INIO and CAT are fully booked through 2028.
tension_points.bear_case: The market debate is whether the industry becomes oversupplied, as many players add capacity and time-to-power constraints may ease.
tension_points.what_invalidates: If unlimited availability of power generation technology removes the time-to-power premium, the ranking shifts toward cost, and reciprocating engines overtake SOFC.

tension_points.bull_case: Grid interconnection takes 5-7 years, retail power prices are rising and political pushback makes mega-campuses harder to build, so smaller onsite-powered inference nodes gain.
tension_points.bear_case: The grid is the lowest-cost power, and CCGTs or the grid are best suited to 1 GW+ mega-sites given economies of scale and proven technology.

theme_stances.key_argument: The grid cannot deliver power fast enough, so time-to-power makes BTM generation a structural shift rather than a bridge.
theme_stances.evidence: Time-to-power is becoming as important as cost-of-power

theme_stances.key_argument: Storage smooths sub-second GPU load swings and is expected to be paired with onsite thermal generation.
theme_stances.evidence: Storage remains the balancing factor for data center power

theme_stances.key_argument: Local opposition, moratoriums and permitting changes push developers toward smaller sites with onsite power.
theme_stances.evidence: Political Pushback Could Support BTM Power
